            Bio
            Hello world! I am a Collegiate
            Assistant Professor at the University of Chicago, where
            I teach Global Society in the College
            Core. Trained as a quantitative social scientist, I do
            interdisciplinary research on demography and population
            health.
            Before joining the University of Chicago, I was a
            postdoctoral scholar at the Center for
            Economic History at Northwestern University. I have a
            PhD in Sustainable
            Development from Columbia University.
            Off campus, you’re most likely to find me wilderness canoeing, enjoying
            the Chicago lake
            shore, or reading sci-fi and fantasy (current
            recommendation).

articles.title: Research
articles.contents:
I study population health in data-scarce settings. One strand of my work develops childhood sex ratios as a proxy for early-life mortality. Because boys die at higher rates in infancy, the sex composition of surviving children can be used as an indicator for stillbirths and infant mortality. I apply this indicator to the historical US, where we lack vital statistics but have excellent census data.
Another strand of my work focuses on maternal-infant health in contemporary sub-Saharan Africa. Using Demographic and Health Survey (DHS) data, I explore how food and water insecurity contribute to child health outcomes.
Publications
Infant Mortality among US Whites in the 19th Century:
New Evidence from Childhood Sex Ratios
with James R. Irwin · Demographic Research 52: 303–350. 2025.

We use childhood sex ratios, which skew female when infant mortality is high, to
estimate 19th-century US infant mortality. For US whites we find roughly 70–80
deaths per 1,000 circa 1850.


Read the article

Child Anemia and the 2008 Food Price Crisis in Senegal ·
Demographic Research 51: 637–668. 2024.

I examine how the 2008 food price crisis affected child hemoglobin in Senegal,
using a natural-experiment comparison of in-utero and breastfeeding children.
I find large negative effects in urban areas, especially Dakar, and none in
rural areas.


Read the article

Working Papers
The Hidden Costs of Mass Deportations:
Early-Life Mortality and the 1930s Mexican Repatriation
with Sergio Eduardo López Araiza Bejar (October 2026)

The repatriation campaign of the 1930s removed a large share of the Mexican-origin
population of the United States, including many US-born children. We use childhood
sex ratios to estimate the effect of this campaign on early-life mortality among Mexican immigrants in Texas.
We find that the campaign caused a major shift toward females among the children of the affected population,
implying a large increase in early-life mortality.


Draft

Works in Progress
Black Health in Slavery and Freedom: New Evidence from Childhood Sex Ratios.
With James R. Irwin. We estimate infant mortality for the US Black populations,
1850–1880, using childhood sex ratios.
Comparing the JMP Drinking Water Ladder and the HWISE Scale in the 2022–23
Mozambique DHS. With Indira Bose, Joshua Miller and Sera Young. We compare an
infrastructure-based and an experience-based measure of household water access in a
single survey. Presented as a poster at the 2026 UNC Water and Health Conference
The Industrialization Puzzle in the US: New Evidence from Childhood Sex Ratios.
I use childhood sex ratios to show that US population health deteriorated across the
period 1850–1910, not just before the Civil War, recasting the “Antebellum Puzzle” as an
“Industrialization Puzzle.”
Sex Ratio at Birth and the HIV Epidemic in South Africa. With Jenny Trinitapoli.
We find that HIV prevalence is associated with female-skewed sex ratios at birth in South
Africa, and could account for roughly half the gap from a biologically normal ratio. This
relationship weakened with the expansion of antiretroviral drugs.

articles.title: Teaching
articles.contents:
I teach the Global Society sequence in the College Core at the University of Chicago. Before this, at Northwestern University, I designed a course in demographic history and co-taught a course on global health methods.
In my classes, students work learn to make and evaluate an argument from primary sources, ranging from Ibn Khaldun’s Muqaddimah to John Graunt’s life tables to census microdata from IPUMS. I want my students to be able to make an argument from scratch, not just repeat summaries.
My classroom approach follows from this: class time is device-free for group exercises and discussion, with laptops only coming out for computing work. Assessment is built so that the work is the student’s own: in-person exams for reading-based courses and original research for the rest.
Core Social Sciences Sequence
Global Society I, II and III — SOSC 16100 / 16200 / 16300 · University of Chicago · 2025–present
Two sections each year, ~15 students each · three quarters from social theory through demographic methods to an independent research paper

Course description and structure
A three-quarter Core social sciences sequence. The first quarter works through works of social theory from around the world, the second teaches demographic methods alongside the intellectual history of population thought, and the third is a supervised research project.
I — Social theory. Classic texts on society, development, inequality and population, such as Ibn Khaldun’s Muqaddimah, Thomas More’s Utopia and Nyerere’s Ujamaa.
II — Population and Society. Three parts. Population thought, reading large-scale studies of global population such as Malthus and McNeill’s Plagues and Peoples. Then demographic methods (Lexis diagrams, standardization and life tables) taught through weekly lab tutorials and problem sets. Then contemporary research on migration, fertility and marriage. Students leave able to construct a life table, standardize a comparison between populations, and look for demographic explanations of social phenomena.
III — Research Practicum. Each student develops an independent project from question formulation to a 4,000–6,000 word paper with a literature review, data and methods, and results. The quarter is scaffolded through a topic survey, research proposal, annotated bibliography, research update, draft figures and draft introduction. It ends with conference-style presentations and Q&A.
Previously, I taught one section of the third quarter as an adjunct lecturer (2023–2024).
Quantitative and Methods Teaching
The Demographic History of the US post 1860 — ECON 323-2 · Northwestern University · Winter 2025
Designed and taught solo · ~65 students · students analyze IPUMS census microdata · ends in an independent research project

Course description
Listed in the catalog as Economic History of the United States since 1865; I designed and taught it as a course in demographic history. The course examines US demographic history from after the Civil War to the mid-twentieth century. Students learn core demographic concepts and measures, explore US demographic patterns and change, and examine leading theories of fertility and mortality decline alongside the role of immigration. They learn to analyze publicly available census microdata from IPUMS, culminating in an independent research project.
Methods in Global Health — ANT 390 · Northwestern University · 2025
Co-taught with Sera Young · ~15 students · I led the statistical computing component using Demographic and Health Survey (DHS) data

Course description
A seminar on quantitative and qualitative methods in global health research. I led the statistical computing component, teaching students to work with DHS data in R and to evaluate measurement choices in global health indicators. The course culminates in an independent research project, presented in a conference-style poster.
